paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana, was a campaign by white farmers and crowds in late May 1903 to drive Black families and laborers from the county after Rosa Kaiser, a white girl, was killed and her father beaten near Manchester station. Black residents were ordered out on penalty of death, families were driven from their homes, and the suspect, Louis Everson, was stoned and chased from Lawrenceburg by a mob. Within days the girl's family and the marshal said the killer may have been white.

Martin Kaiser, 73, and his daughter, given as Rosa and seventeen, were walking home from Ascension day services at Yorkville on the evening of May 21 when both were attacked. According to the first Lawrenceburg dispatch, Kaiser said a Black man had clubbed him and carried off his daughter; posses with bloodhounds took up the search, and the correspondent predicted a lynching. Her body was found in Tanner's creek on May 23 with the skull crushed. Large gangs of Black laborers were then working on Big Four railroad improvements nearby.

Everson, known as "Black Ponto," was held in the Lawrenceburg jail on suspicion. On May 24 farmers gathered in several towns and openly threatened lynching, and a wire account said he escaped only because a Manchester witness did not identify him. Released for lack of evidence on May 25 and escorted beyond the city limits, he was followed for a mile by men and boys who cursed, stoned and beat him; the Courier-Journal added that shots were fired after him.

The campaign meanwhile turned against the county's Black population as a whole. An Indianapolis dispatch of May 24 reported that all Black people were ordered to leave within three days or face death, and that seven families near Manchester station had been driven from homes the mob nearly burned. A brother of the dead girl circulated a petition against Black labor, and on May 26 a farmers' committee led by Martin J. Kaiser, Jr., told the Big Four foreman at Guilford that his Black workers must go. A May 27 dispatch estimated that 100 Black people had been driven from the rural districts in three days.

By May 26 Kaiser and the girl's uncle, Frank Aust, believed the attacker was white, Aust saying he was "closer at home than any negro," and the marshal later called the Black suspect's alibi complete. On September 2 the murder was still unsolved, and the sheriff was seeking Otto Pool, a former Big Four worker wanted for grand larceny. No report of action against those who drove out Black residents or attacked Everson appears in the coverage. In October a Lawrenceburg dispatch still traced Black workers' fear of mobs to the Kaiser murder.

The first wire story, "Posses Out With Dogs" in the Indianapolis Journal, was still appearing in Texas in June. The New York Sun's "Driving Out the Negroes" dispatch said there was "no doubt" a Black man was the killer, though an Indiana weekly printed the same text as "Revenge on Innocent Negroes." The Indianapolis Journal called expulsion "certainly unreasonable," and the Indianapolis News made the episode a lesson against lynching and against treating people of one color as "predisposed to crime."

Southern papers used it against the North. Bill Arp's Atlanta Constitution column hailed Indiana as "the champion state for lynching negroes," and a Wilmington Messenger paragraph on "Northern Republican" Indiana circulated in Georgia and South Carolina. A Macon letter in the Sun condoned the hunt for the accused but deplored punishing an entire Black community.

Black papers ran short items. The Savannah Tribune reprinted the wire as "Making War on Negroes," and the St. Paul Appeal mocked Manchester's "best citizens," whose drive against Black railroad hands would have to stop because the crime was "done by a Caucasian."

The first dispatch had Kaiser describing a Black attacker; the family soon said he was white; a September report said Kaiser never saw him. Local specials named the girl Rosa, aged seventeen, while wire copy called her Anna and one paper gave her age as thirty. Counts of those expelled ranged from seven families to 100 people to "hundreds."

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana
bases: The core acts were orders for all Black residents to leave the county on penalty of death, families driven from their homes, and demands that contractors and farmers discharge Black workers (A10, A15, A18); the mobbing of the suspect Everson was part of the same campaign (A12, A14).

The Indianapolis Journal's Lawrenceburg specials, the Courier-Journal, and separate Indianapolis wire dispatches agree on the threats, the driving out of Black families and workers, and the mobbing of Everson (A10, A12, A13, A15, A18).

accounts.label: First Lawrenceburg dispatch
accounts.gist: Kaiser, on regaining consciousness, said a Black man clubbed him and carried his daughter into the woods, and gave a detailed description; lynching was expected if the man was caught.

accounts.label: Indianapolis wire (May 24-27)
accounts.gist: White residents ordered all Black people out of the county on penalty of death, drove seven families from their homes, and forced the discharge of Black workers; about 100 were driven out in three days.

accounts.label: Lawrenceburg specials on Everson
accounts.gist: Everson was spared lynching only because he was not identified, then was released and chased from town by a mob that stoned, beat and shot at him.

accounts.label: Kaiser family and officials (later)
accounts.gist: By May 26 the father and uncle believed the attacker was white; the marshal called the suspected Black man's alibi complete; in September the father was said not to have seen the assailant at all.

accounts.label: Black press comment
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Appeal said the campaign by Manchester's 'best citizens' must stop since the crime was shown to be a white man's.

framing.detail: Early wire copy ('Posses Out With Dogs', 'Driving Out the Negroes') stated there was 'no doubt' a Black man was the killer, while an Indiana paper ran the same wire as 'Revenge on Innocent Negroes.'
The Indianapolis Journal called expulsion 'unreasonable' and the Indianapolis News made it a lesson against lynching, whitecapping and racial presumption.

Southern columns mocked Indiana as the 'champion state for lynching negroes' and used the expulsion against the 'Northern Republican' state, while a Macon letter condoned the hunt for the accused but deplored punishing a whole community.
The Savannah Tribune ran the wire as 'Making War on Negroes'; the St. Paul Appeal put 'best citizens' in quotation marks and noted the crime was 'done by a Caucasian.'
